newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to reopen aging Soviet-era cosmodrome.
newsitem.headline: Russia to reopen aging Soviet-era cosmodrome.

text.p: Russia plans to reopen a top-secret Soviet-era space launching pad which has been closed for the past 11 years, an official at a rocket making company said on Tuesday.
The first launch from Kapustin Yar (Cabbage Ravine), near the Caspian Sea, was planned for February 1999, the official from the Siberia-based rocket design bureau Polyot said.
In the first scheduled launch, a light booster Kosmos-3M rocket will put a German astronomy satellite into orbit.
The official, who asked not to be identified, also said that launches from Kapustin Yar achieved an ideal suborbital trajectory for a rocket's flight.
Kapustin Yar was a top-secret Soviet rocket launching pad from where 139 military and civil rockets were launched between 1961 and 1988.
It is owned by the military's Strategic Rocket Forces, which cannot afford to run it.
A spokesman for the strategic forces declined to comment on the deal with Polyot.
But a spokesman at the Military Space Forces, which is also part of the defence ministry, said that Kapustin Yar was not suitable for commercial launches because it was too close to populated areas.
"There are a lot of people who live in the zone where the rocket stages fall...and they (the stages) could fall on the territory of foreign states," spokesman Sergei Gorbunov said.
Officials say another new Russian cosmodrome, Svobodny in the Far East, is more likely to be used for commercial satellites.
Military Space Force deputy commander Vladimir Durnev said recently that two Western probes would be launched from Svobodny by the end of 1997.
"We plan to launch a U.S.-made probe in June and a Swedish communications satellite later this year," Durnev told a news conference last week.
Russia made a test launch of a military probe from Svobodny in March using Start-1, a modernized SS-25 intercontinental ballistic missile.
But the launch sparked protests from enviromentalists in Yakutia, who warned that discarded stages of the booster rocket could damage the environment.
Yuri Baturin, secretary of Russia's Defence Council, said Svobodny would be attractive to the South East Asian market nearby for commercial launches.

"It (Svobodny) is not a competitor to the Baikonur cosmodrome now, but it is very promising for commercial launches," Baturin said after the test rocket was launched from the cosmodrome in the Far Eastern taiga.

The Kremlin developed the Baikonur cosmodrome as its main space facility from the mid-1950s. But Kazakhstan became independent when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991 and Russia has been charged for access to the facility.
Russia has a contract for $115 million annually to use Baikonur but so far has declined to pay its bills, and is actively seeking alternative launch sites.
